newsitem.title: DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC OF CONGO: U.N. massacre probe seeks cooperation in ex-Zaire.
newsitem.headline: U.N. massacre probe seeks cooperation in ex-Zaire.

text.p: U.N. investigators arrived in Congo's capital Kinshasa on Friday to probe alleged massacres of Rwandan Hutu refugees by new leader Laurent Kabila's forces or their regional allies.
The head of the small advance team said he was confident of help from the new authorities despite a U.S. newspaper report that Kabila had instructed them not to offer assistance.
"I am expecting good cooperation," Georg Mautner-Markhof of the U.N. human rights organisation told reporters on arrival at Kinshasa airport.
"We are here because Mr Kabila gave assurances that his government was ready to help and we hope that is still the case," his spokesman John Wills said later.

The mission follows persistent allegations of massacres deep in the jungles of what was then Zaire by Kabila's rebel forces, who ousted president Mobutu Sese Seko in May, and their Tutsi allies from Rwanda and Burundi.
The advance party of six, to be joined by two colleagues later on Friday, includes two forensic experts.
"We had a brief meeting here today with (U.N. special envoy ambassador Mohamed) Sahnoun and have talked to the (aid) agencies, and we are letting the government know we are here," Mills said.
The team hopes to talk to Kabila and his officials as soon as possible and to visit areas where the investigations will take place before the full mission arrives on July 7.

Mills said the full team's size would depend on the negotiations with the Congo over freedom of movement. In May, U.N. investigators failed to gain access to the east of the Congo on a planned reconnaissance trip.

The U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees says more than 200,000 Hutu refugees who had been living in Zaire for more than two years are unaccounted for. Some 800,000 went home to Rwanda after their camps were overrun by Kabila's men.
The arrival of Mautner-Markhof's team was clouded by a Washington Post report that Kabila has told some local officials to do as little as possible to aid it.

Citing unnamed Western and Congolese sources, it said Kabila had told officials in the east near the border with Rwanda, Uganda and Burundi, "not to direct human rights investigators to any mass grave sites or potential witnesses".

The sources said Kabila was under intense pressure from Rwandan and Ugandan officials to stymie the probe. Security units from the two countries played an important part in Kabila's armed uprising that began in October.
In exchange for help to topple Mobutu, Kabila was forced to give those units a free hand in gunning down thousands of ethnic Hutu refugees, the sources were quoted as saying.

Kabila's own army also included ethnic Tutsis, traditional rivals of the Hutus who fled Rwanda in 1994 after the genocide of up to a million people from the Tutsi minority that later wrested control of the country.
The United States did not accept the reports that Kabila may try to hinder the investigation. "We expect him to keep his word and we fully expect him to cooperate," a spokesman said.
He said Assistant Secretary of State John Shattuck, who oversees human rights issues, was promised full cooperation last week by Rwandan Vice President Paul Kagame.
